paragraphs: Before the next rehearsal, the director asked members to check a short example message. It named a proposed meeting time, the reason it might change, and the date when another update would be sent. One reader initially understood that date as a promise that permission would have arrived by then. The director changed the wording to make clear that it was a date for checking, not a guarantee of approval. Being more specific about an update did not remove the uncertainty about the event itself.

The team then put a status beside each scene in the shared table. When someone copied a time into another message, the status and the latest update date were to travel with it. Older versions were marked so that members could see which information had been replaced. These changes did not prevent bad weather or ensure that every plan would succeed. They made it easier to tell the difference between a working plan and a commitment, while giving people a clear place to check before making changes to their own travel and family arrangements.
rationale: tentativeを確定状態・更新予定日の区別で読み取る。過去完了、受動態、関係節、形式目的語と情報の持ち出しを扱う。

paragraphs: Before introducing the shorter process, the receptionist watched two applicants complete a trial version. One used the website, while the other chose the paper application. Both could finish without entering the same address twice. However, the paper applicant was unsure whether a separate online account was also required. The school added a clear statement that either application route was acceptable.

Staff also checked whether the shorter signature sheet still identified the application it belonged to. Removing repeated details would not help if a signature could no longer be matched to the right record. They kept a simple reference number for that purpose rather than asking for the full address again.

After the first week, the manager reviewed common questions from applicants and mistakes reported by staff. A shorter form was not automatically a clearer one. The aim was to remove repetition that served no useful function while retaining the information and routes people actually needed. The school judged the change by how the whole process worked, not merely by the number of boxes it had deleted.

paragraphs: Before the trial began, students worked with staff to describe what caring for the approved plants would involve each week. The list included routine tasks and a way to report problems to the responsible adult. It also asked who would be available during school holidays. A plan that depended on one enthusiastic student being present every day would not become workable simply because the drawing used fewer containers. The practical question concerned the continuing work as well as the first installation.

During the trial, the committee kept notes on the time and materials actually needed. Students discovered that their first estimate of the work had been too optimistic. They revised the care schedule before proposing any expansion. Success in the agreed area would not show that the whole roof could support the original design. Any larger phase would still need the relevant checks and permission. The smaller project gave them experience for a better proposal, rather than a reason to treat every remaining condition as settled. In this sense, feasibility was something to examine as the plan developed, not a label that ended all further questions.

paragraphs: For the revised report, staff first agreed what would count as observed use of a corridor panel. Walking past it and stopping to read it were recorded separately. They also kept notes on the times when each space had been observed. A quiet morning session could not automatically represent a busy afternoon. The observation schedule was included so readers could judge coverage. These details helped readers understand the scope of the figures instead of treating them as a complete count of everyone interested in local history.

The team then noticed another difficulty: someone could enter the main room and later stop in the corridor. Adding the two totals would not necessarily give the number of different visitors. The report therefore described observations of use, not a verified total of unique people. This distinction did not make the corridor activity unimportant. It made the claim fit the evidence. The library planned a later study if it needed a different measure, rather than stretching the current figures to answer a question they had not been designed to address.
rationale: overlookedを集計方法と範囲から推測する。知覚構文、関係節、受動態、動名詞主語と実人数・観察数の区別を扱う。

paragraphs: At the review meeting, a shopkeeper explained that she had helped every evening but could not continue at that pace. Her neighbors had seen her shop open and assumed that she no longer needed support. The association recorded remaining needs separately from whether a business had reopened. Returning to work did not necessarily mean that losses had been recovered or that the owner had enough time to rest.

Members also asked who could take each task and for how long. A name on a contact list was not a promise of unlimited help. The list included ways to update availability, and requests that could not be met were kept visible rather than treated as failures of community spirit.

The next report described achievements alongside the work still unfinished. It recognized cooperation without expecting a few volunteers to carry every burden. The association continued seeking appropriate outside assistance where local resources were insufficient. Resilience described an ability to respond and learn; it did not require people to hide exhaustion or pretend that support was no longer necessary.
rationale: resilientを協力と残る負担の見直しから読む。関係節、部分否定、間接疑問、動名詞主語と支援の限界を扱う。
